prompt.context: Our client is Rotisserie Ranch, a poultry farming company that specializes in growing chickens for rotisserie roasting. Its main line customer segment is comprised of large grocery chains, who buy its chickens to fresh roast in the meat departments of their grocery stores. Market research has revealed to Rotisserie Ranch that more and more consumers have begun buying flavored rotisserie chickens recently.
prompt.question: Rotisserie Ranch is thinking of pre-flavoring some of its chickens for grocers. Should Rotisserie Ranch begin selling this new product?

clarifying_info.q: What is the competitive landscape for pre-seasoned rotisserie chicken?
clarifying_info.a: For the purposes of this case, Rotisserie Ranch will only compete against existing Private Label brands at grocery stores. No other competitor can enter the pre-seasoned market because Rotisserie Ranch has a patented process for sterilely packaging chicken so it stays fresh for 30 days without freezing — competitors who freeze chicken cannot pre-season it.

clarifying_info.q: What is Rotisserie Ranch's market position?
clarifying_info.a: Rotisserie Ranch is currently the industry market share leader in rotisserie-ready chicken.
Four new flavored products to be introduced concurrently: Barbecue, Lemon Herb, Tandoori, and Teriyaki.

clarifying_info.q: What happens to unsold cooked chickens at the end of the day?
clarifying_info.a: Predicting demand for cooked chickens is difficult for grocers; any leftover cooked chickens at the end of the day are thrown out. Unthawed chickens cannot be re-frozen.

exhibits.title: Market Test of Pre-Seasoned BBQ Chicken
exhibits.shows: A demand curve chart for the Rotisserie Ranch market test of Pre-Seasoned BBQ Chicken, plotting Price (P) on the y-axis and Quantity (Q) on the x-axis. Two data points are labeled: Point A (Q=400, P=$4.00) and Point B (Q=1000, P=$3.00). Both stores have a 25% Retailer Margin noted.

exhibits.title: Control Group Stores
exhibits.shows: A table comparing two control group stores selling Standard Rotisserie chicken alongside two test stores selling Store-Seasoned Rotisserie chicken. Provides weekly sales revenue, retail price, seasoning cost, and retailer margin for each. The retailer margin for the seasoned stores is left blank (marked '?') for the candidate to calculate.

framework: Value to customers (grocery chains): Will grocers want to buy and stock pre-seasoned chickens?
Revenue and cost implications: Does the price increase to grocers offset the cost increase to Rotisserie Ranch?
Market testing: How do we verify consumer demand before a full rollout?
Competition: Are there competitors in the pre-seasoned segment, and how does Rotisserie Ranch's competitive position hold?

questions.prompt: Do you think that grocery retailers would be interested in pre-seasoned chickens from Rotisserie Ranch?
questions.guidance: No single correct answer; must be logically defended. Strong YES arguments: (1) Labor Cost Reduction — meat department workers don't need to spend time seasoning chickens; (2) Economies of Scale — centralized seasoning lowers unit cost; (3) Product Consistency — centrally managed R&D yields better, more consistent flavor. Strong NO arguments: (1) Loss of Differentiation — grocery chains differentiate via value-added in-store activities; (2) Better Attuned to Local Tastes — grocers may better gauge local consumer preferences; (3) Increases Inventory and SKUs — more complexity in store operations.

questions.prompt: Grocers are interested in the product but want to be sure the chickens will sell well. How would you make sure?
questions.guidance: The correct answer is to run a test market (pilot study). Candidate should identify that: (1) a pilot test should be run in a representative sample of stores; (2) the pilot needs a control or comparison group so results can be attributed to the new product, not other factors. Cut the candidate off once they demonstrate understanding of these two points.

questions.prompt: A test market launch for the new Rotisserie Ranch BBQ chicken was administered (hand out Exhibit 1). Should the grocers carry our product? Calculate the gross profit per store from the test.
questions.guidance: Candidate must calculate retail margin and gross profit for each test store. They should then recognize they cannot determine whether to recommend the product with only test store data — they need a control group to compare against. This should prompt them to ask for Exhibit 2.

math.setup: Retail Margin ($) = Retailer Margin % x Retail Price. Gross Profit = Margin per unit x Units Sold.
steps: Store A: Retail Margin = 25% x $4.00 = $1.00 per unit
Store A: Gross Profit = $1.00 x 400 units = $400
Store B: Retail Margin = 25% x $3.00 = $0.75 per unit
Store B: Gross Profit = $0.75 x 1,000 units = $750
Cannot make a recommendation without a control group — must ask for Exhibit 2.
math.answer: Store A gross profit = $400; Store B gross profit = $750. Insufficient to decide without control data.

questions.prompt: Using the control group data (Exhibit 2), calculate the variable margin and gross profit for both standard and store-seasoned rotisserie chickens. Should grocers shift to Rotisserie Ranch's pre-seasoned product?
questions.guidance: Candidate must calculate variable margin for standard rotisserie (using 30% margin and no seasoning cost) and for store-seasoned (using 30% margin minus $0.20/$0.15 seasoning cost). Compare gross profits between the test stores (Exhibit 1) and the comparable control stores (Exhibit 2). An excellent candidate notes that Rotisserie Ranch's pre-seasoned chicken yields $100-$150 more gross profit than the store-seasoned alternative. An excellent candidate also interpolates the linear demand function: at $3.50 price point, sales = 700 units, variable margin = $0.875/unit, gross profit = $612.50.

math.setup: Variable Margin ($) = (Retailer Margin % x Retail Price) - Seasoning Cost. Gross Profit = Variable Margin x Units Sold. Units Sold = Weekly Sales / Retail Price.
steps: Standard Rotisserie — Store 1: Units = $1,000 / $3.33 ≈ 300 units; Margin = 30% x $3.33 - $0.00 = $1.00/unit; Gross Profit = $1.00 x 300 = $300
Standard Rotisserie — Store 2: Units = $2,000 / $2.50 = 800 units; Margin = 30% x $2.50 - $0.00 = $0.75/unit; Gross Profit = $0.75 x 800 = $600
Store-Seasoned — Store 1 (comparable to test Store A): Units = $1,200 / $3.99 ≈ 300 units; Margin = 30% x $3.99 - $0.20 = $1.00/unit; Gross Profit = $1.00 x 300 = $300
Store-Seasoned — Store 2 (comparable to test Store B): Units = $2,400 / $2.99 ≈ 803 units ≈ 800 units; Margin = 30% x $2.99 - $0.15 = $0.75/unit; Gross Profit = $0.75 x 800 = $600
Comparison: Test Store A (Rotisserie Ranch BBQ) gross profit = $400 vs Control Store 1 (store-seasoned) gross profit = $300 → incremental gain = $100 (33.3% increase)
Test Store B gross profit = $750 vs Control Store 2 gross profit = $600 → incremental gain = $150 (25% increase)
math.answer: Both standard and store-seasoned rotisserie chickens yield the same variable margins ($1.00 and $0.75/unit). Rotisserie Ranch's pre-seasoned BBQ chicken generates $100-$150 more gross profit per store per week than the current store-seasoned alternative (33.3% and 25% increases respectively). Grocer should carry the product.

recommendation: Rotisserie Ranch should launch the Pre-Seasoned BBQ Chicken product and test the other three flavors (Lemon Herb, Tandoori, Teriyaki) because market demand is shifting toward seasoned rotisserie chicken and the test market confirms a clear financial benefit to grocers.

Grocers can expect $100-$150 more gross profit per store per week by switching from their own store-seasoned product to Rotisserie Ranch's pre-seasoned product, representing a 25-33% operating profit improvement.

Cannibalization of the standard rotisserie chicken line is not an issue: variable margins and gross profits are the same on standard and store-seasoned rotisserie chicken, so shifting to the new product is a net benefit in all scenarios.

Assuming the price increase to grocers offsets the increased cost of production (seasoning), Rotisserie Ranch benefits from increased sales volume and potential scale economies over time as pre-seasoned chicken volumes grow.
risks: If the test markets were not representative, actual sales results may differ — full rollout should be staged.
Rotisserie Ranch's cost increase from seasoning must be fully passed through to grocers; if grocers resist the price premium, margins could be squeezed.
Managing four new SKUs simultaneously increases operational complexity for both Rotisserie Ranch and grocers.
Consumer preference for specific flavors is regional; not all four flavors may perform equally across markets.
next_steps: Stage the rollout: launch BBQ first (confirmed by test market), then expand to other three flavors as results are gathered.
Negotiate pricing with grocery chains to ensure the seasoning cost is fully offset in the wholesale price.
Monitor for any competitive response (e.g., private label brands attempting alternative preservation methods).
Quantify potential labor savings to grocers from outsourcing the seasoning step — use this as an additional selling point.
Track cannibalization of standard rotisserie line sales to confirm the assumption holds at scale.
